passage:
Dear Imran,
You asked why I've been missing our morning walks. Honestly? I haven't been sleeping. I start a game "for twenty minutes" at ten and look up at two. My eyes feel full of sand in first period. Last week I fell asleep in chemistry and Ma'am had to tap my desk. I was so embarrassed 😔
The weird part is I don't even enjoy the last hours. I'm just stuck doing one more round.
So I'm trying something. The laptop now charges in Mummy's room after ten. I told her myself. I set an alarm at 9:45 as a warning. Tonight was the first try and I was restless, but I slept by eleven.
Walk tomorrow? 6:30, the usual gate.
Ankita

qa.q: Where does Ankita's laptop charge after ten now?
qa.a: It charges in Mummy's room.

qa.q: How did Ankita feel after falling asleep in chemistry?
qa.a: Ankita felt embarrassed when Ma'am had to tap the desk, which helped Ankita see that the late gaming was causing real trouble.

qa.q: Why might Ankita's plan work better than just promising to stop?
qa.a: Moving the laptop and setting a warning alarm put a physical limit in place, so Ankita doesn't rely on willpower at 10 pm.

qa.q: How might Imran feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Imran might be relieved to know why Ankita skipped the walks, happy to meet again, and glad Ankita was honest.

grounding: It shows a teen noticing that gaming has pushed out sleep and setting personal limits.

passage: So you want to know how bad it got? Okay. I'm Harsha, I'm sixteen, and three months ago I was scrolling till three every night. Not even fun stuff, just scrolling. My sister Minakshi noticed first. She shares my room and said my screen lit up the whole ceiling. I told her to mind her business. But then I failed a test I'd actually studied for, because I couldn't think straight. That scared me. I checked my screen time and it was, like, seven hours a day. I didn't believe it. Now I keep the phone across the room so I have to get up. I still slip sometimes. But I sleep more, and Minakshi says I'm less grumpy in the mornings, which, honestly, rude. But true.

qa.q: Who noticed Harsha's late-night scrolling first?
qa.a: Harsha's sister Minakshi, who shares the room, noticed first.

qa.q: Why did failing the test scare Harsha?
qa.a: Harsha had studied, so failing showed that the lost sleep was hurting clear thinking, not just mood.

qa.q: What could Harsha add if the slips keep happening some nights?
qa.a: Harsha could set a fixed time to put the phone away each night and maybe ask Minakshi for reminders, without being harsh about slips.

qa.q: How might Minakshi see the change in Harsha?
qa.a: She probably finds the room darker and quieter at night and Harsha easier to be around, and may feel glad she spoke up. 🙂

grounding: A teen describes noticing compulsive scrolling and its effect on sleep and marks, then setting a limit.

passage: I'm Rukmini, and Madhav is the boy next door. We've taken the same school bus since we were small. This year he started sleeping on it, head against the window, mouth open. He missed his stop twice. His mother told mine he gamed with friends online till late, sometimes till the birds started. Last month something shifted. I saw him at the bus stop with a paperback, yawning but awake. He said his friends now log off at eleven together; they made a rule so no one feels left out. He still looked tired on Mondays. Once I heard him tell his little brother, "Phone down, bed. I'm serious." I don't know how hard it was for him, but he hasn't missed his stop since.

qa.q: How many times did Madhav miss his stop?
qa.a: He missed his stop twice.

qa.q: What might Madhav's still-tired Mondays suggest?
qa.a: They suggest he may still slip on weekends, and that keeping the limit is an ongoing effort rather than a finished change.

qa.q: Why did the friends' shared log-off rule work well?
qa.a: Logging off together at eleven meant no one feared missing out, so it was easier for Madhav to stop.

qa.q: How might Madhav's little brother feel being told "Phone down, bed"?
qa.a: He might feel annoyed at being bossed, but he may also sense his brother is serious because he knows how it feels.

grounding: A neighbour observes a teen's gaming cutting into his sleep and the limit he sets with friends.

passage: Week one: Anjali, sixteen, yawned through the first period every day. She'd been watching short videos in bed until two. 'Just one more,' she'd tell herself, forty times. Her brother Joseph teased, 'Panda eyes!' She didn't laugh. Week two, Sunday: She checked her screen-time page and felt sick. Five hours after eleven p.m. across the week. She wrote on a sticky note: 'Phone charges in the hall at 11. Alarm clock, not phone.' Joseph raised an eyebrow. 'You'll last one night.' Week four: She had slipped twice, once for a cricket final, and started again the next day both times. First period felt different now. 'No panda eyes,' Joseph admitted, and she threw a pillow at him.

qa.q: What rule did Anjali write on her sticky note?
qa.a: The phone charges in the hall at 11, and she uses an alarm clock, not her phone.

qa.q: What did Anjali feel when she checked her screen-time page?
qa.a: She felt sick, shocked by how many late-night hours she was losing.

qa.q: What went right after Anjali slipped?
qa.a: She restarted the limit the very next day instead of giving up entirely.

qa.q: How might Joseph's view of his sister's plan change over the weeks?
qa.a: He went from doubting she'd last a night to admitting the change was working.

grounding: Over several weeks a teen notices compulsive late-night scrolling and sets a personal limit.

passage: Kamal, you think your Nani doesn't understand games? Let me tell you about your Suresh mama. When he was fifteen, a video game parlour opened near our market. Ten coins a game. He began going after school, then instead of tuition. He'd come home at night saying he'd been at a friend's. His eyes were red, he slept in class. One day his teacher came to our house. I wasn't angry first; I was frightened. He cried and said, 'Amma, I can't stop, I keep thinking about the next level.' We made a plan together: the parlour only on Sundays, and I'd walk him to tuition. He hated it for a month. Then he got better at studies, and cricket. You see the tiredness in your own eyes, beta?

qa.q: What did Suresh start skipping to go to the parlour?
qa.a: He began going to the parlour instead of tuition.

qa.q: What did Suresh feel when he told his mother he couldn't stop?
qa.a: He felt out of control and upset, crying because he kept thinking about the next level.

qa.q: What worked in the plan Suresh and his mother made?
qa.a: It set a clear limit together, only Sundays, and added support by walking him to tuition.

qa.q: How might Kamal feel hearing that Suresh mama struggled in the same way?
qa.a: Kamal might feel less judged and more willing to look honestly at their own tiredness and gaming.

grounding: A grandmother recalls a teen noticing compulsive gaming and setting limits with family help.

passage:
The history exam was at eight the next morning, and at 1:40 a.m. Mahima, sixteen, was still scrolling.
She'd opened her phone “for five minutes” at eleven. Now her eyes stung and she remembered nothing from chapter six.
Her brother Siddharth knocked. “Your light's still on.”
“I know,” she snapped. Then, more quietly, “I can't stop.”
He held out his hand. “Give it. I'll put it on the fridge.”
She hesitated, then handed it over.
In the morning, tired but less foggy, she wrote on a sticky note: Phone on fridge at 10. Every night. She stuck it on her mirror.
She passed, barely. That night at ten, she walked the phone to the fridge herself.

qa.q: What time was the history exam?
qa.a: At eight the next morning.

qa.q: How did Mahima feel when she said “I can't stop”?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and helpless, aware she was stuck in scrolling.

qa.q: What limit did Mahima set, and why might it work?
qa.a: Putting the phone on the fridge at ten every night, because the phone is out of reach at bedtime.

qa.q: How does Siddharth help his sister?
qa.a: He notices the light, offers to take the phone and supports her without lecturing.

grounding: The night before an exam a sixteen-year-old notices compulsive scrolling and sets a personal limit.

passage:
Tenzin, fifteen, had been gaming until one or two most nights. In the mornings in their Darjeeling flat, his mother Bidisha had to shake him awake.
At football practice on Thursday, he missed an easy pass and the coach said, “Where's your head?” Tenzin didn't know.
That weekend, he checked his phone's screen-time page. Five hours on Saturday alone.
He felt a sting of shame. He went to his mother. “Can the console live in the living room? And can you switch the wifi off at eleven?”
Bidisha looked surprised. “Your idea?”
“Mine.”
A week later, he scored in practice. He was asleep by 11:30 most nights.

qa.q: What did the coach say when Tenzin missed a pass?
qa.a: “Where's your head?”

qa.q: How did Tenzin feel when he saw five hours of screen time?
qa.a: He felt a sting of shame.

qa.q: What limits did Tenzin choose, and why are they effective?
qa.a: Moving the console to the living room and switching the wifi off at eleven, which makes late gaming harder.

qa.q: How did Bidisha react to Tenzin's request?
qa.a: She was surprised and probably pleased that it was his own idea.

grounding: A fifteen-year-old notices gaming displacing sleep and sets his own limits.

passage:
“Bro, look at this.” Eshaan held up his phone. “Screen time: seven hours yesterday.”
Vikas laughed. “Mine's worse. Eight.”
“That's a full school day. Of scrolling.”
Vikas stopped laughing. “When did I even do that?”
“In bed. I keep saying one more video. Then it's two a.m.”
“Same. I've been falling asleep in chemistry.”
Eshaan thought. “Pact? Phones out of our rooms after eleven. We text each other a photo of the phone on the kitchen table.”
“And if one of us breaks it?”
“Buys the other samosas for a week.”
Vikas held out his hand. “Deal. But I'm not losing samosas to you.”

qa.q: How many hours of screen time did Eshaan have yesterday?
qa.a: Seven hours.

qa.q: How did Vikas feel when he realised eight hours was a full school day?
qa.a: He felt surprised and uneasy, no longer laughing.

qa.q: What makes the friends' pact likely to work?
qa.a: It sets a clear limit, uses proof with a photo, and adds a fun penalty, so they hold each other accountable.

qa.q: How does Vikas's view of his screen time change during the talk?
qa.a: He moves from laughing about it to realising it is a real problem affecting his sleep.

grounding: Two seventeen-year-olds notice compulsive phone use and set personal limits together.

passage:
Last term, I was a zombie. I'd go to bed at eleven, then scroll until two or three. Funny videos, then gaming streams, then more videos. I'd tell myself "five more minutes" about forty times.
In the mornings, I was snappy. I fell asleep in chemistry. My brother Vikas said, "Your eyes look like a panda's."
One night I checked my screen-time report. Six hours after ten p.m. in one week. I felt sick.
So I did something simple. My phone charges in the kitchen now. I bought a cheap alarm clock. The first few nights I lay awake, bored. By the second week, I was falling asleep before midnight.
I'm Sarika, and I'm still not perfect. But I'm not a panda anymore.

qa.q: Where does Sarika's phone charge now?
qa.a: In the kitchen.

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling when seeing the screen-time report?
qa.a: Sarika felt shocked and a bit sick at how much sleep the phone had taken.

qa.q: What simple limit worked for Sarika?
qa.a: Charging the phone in the kitchen and using an alarm clock removed the temptation to scroll in bed.

qa.q: How might Vikas see the change in Sarika?
qa.a: Vikas probably notices Sarika is less snappy and more awake in the mornings.

grounding: A teen looks back on compulsive late-night scrolling and the limit that helped.

passage:
Athletics coach's note, February.
Hansa is one of my best 400 m runners, but for three weeks her times have been dropping. She yawns during warm-up and snapped at a teammate.
Today I asked her about sleep. She admitted she plays online games with friends until two most nights, because "everyone's online then."
I didn't lecture. I asked her what she thought. She said, "I feel terrible in the mornings, but when I'm playing, I don't notice the time."
We agreed on a trial: gaming till ten, then phone out of the room, for two weeks. Her friend Akash on the team said he'd do it too.
I'll check her times next Friday. — Coach Menon

qa.q: Until what time does Hansa play online games most nights?
qa.a: Until two.

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling when she admitted she plays until two?
qa.a: Hansa felt a bit guilty and tired, knowing it was hurting her running.

qa.q: Why might Coach Menon's approach work better than a lecture?
qa.a: Asking Hansa what she thought let her notice the problem herself and agree to a limit she chose.

qa.q: How might Akash's promise affect Hansa?
qa.a: Having a friend join the limit makes it easier to stick to, since she's not missing out alone.

grounding: A coach notes a teen athlete noticing that late gaming hurts her and agreeing a limit.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Day 1 of tracking my screen time. I thought I used my phone maybe two hours a day. The app said five hours forty minutes. Most of it after 10 p.m. Scrolling. I don't even remember what I saw.
Varun says he's the same, and we're making a deal: phones off at 10:30, and we message each other "done" when we turn off.
Day 4: I forgot and scrolled till one. Felt awful at school.
Day 7: Did it 5 out of 7 nights. I actually finished a book. I'd forgotten I liked reading.
It's weird. I don't feel like I'm missing anything. I feel like I got something back.
— Hemant

qa.q: How much screen time did the app show on Day 1?
qa.a: Five hours forty minutes.

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling on Day 4?
qa.a: Hemant felt awful and disappointed after forgetting and scrolling till one.

qa.q: What helped Hemant stick to the limit most nights?
qa.a: The deal with Varun, messaging "done" at 10:30, made it a shared promise.

qa.q: How might Varun be affected by the deal?
qa.a: Varun gets the same support, so both of them are more likely to keep the limit.

grounding: In a diary a teen tracks compulsive phone use and sets a shared limit.

passage:
In Kalimpong, Tenzin's family had one smartphone, and after dinner it was his. He played a football game on it until the battery died, usually after midnight.
One morning at the bus stand, Hafsa had to shake him awake. At school he fell asleep on his arms during history, and Madam asked him to wash his face. His cheeks burned.
That evening he watched himself. He picked up the phone at 8 for "two matches". At 11 his mother said, "Tenzin, the whole house is asleep." He hadn't noticed the time at all.
He felt a bit scared by that. So he made a rule and told his mother about it: the phone charges in the kitchen at 10, with her. The first night he lay awake, itchy. By the fourth night he was asleep before the dogs started barking.

qa.q: Where does the phone charge under Tenzin's new rule?
qa.a: The phone charges in the kitchen at 10, with his mother.

qa.q: Why did Tenzin feel scared when his mother spoke at 11?
qa.a: Tenzin felt uneasy and a bit scared because he hadn't noticed three hours pass at all, which showed how much the game had hold of him.

qa.q: What else could help Tenzin keep his limit?
qa.a: He could plan something calm to do after ten, like reading, and ask his mother or Hafsa to remind him if he slips.

qa.q: How might Hafsa see Tenzin's change?
qa.a: Hafsa would probably be glad not to have to shake him awake at the bus stand any more.

grounding: Shows a teen noticing that gaming was displacing sleep and setting a limit with his family.

passage:
Astrid lived in Tromsø, where in December the sun didn't come up at all. That made it easy to lose track of time. She'd get into bed at ten with the video app and look up at two.
One Monday, her friend Tuan said, "You look like a ghost." She laughed but felt awful. She checked her phone's screen report: almost four hours after 10 p.m., every night.
She tried an experiment. For one week, the phone stayed on her desk across the room, with an alarm clock instead. She read a paper book in bed, even though the first nights she kept reaching for the bedside table out of habit.
On Friday she noticed she'd answered three questions in maths. Tuan noticed too. "Who are you?"
"Someone who sleeps," Astrid said.

qa.q: How long did Astrid's phone report show after 10 p.m.?
qa.a: Almost four hours after 10 p.m., every night.

qa.q: How did Astrid feel when Tuan said she looked like a ghost?
qa.a: She laughed but felt awful, worried about how tired she had become.

qa.q: Which part of Astrid's experiment helped most, and why?
qa.a: Keeping the phone across the room with an alarm clock helped, because the phone wasn't within reach when the habit kicked in.

qa.q: How might Tuan see Astrid on Friday?
qa.a: Tuan seems surprised and pleased, joking "Who are you?" because she is suddenly awake and answering in class.

grounding: Illustrates a teen using a screen-time report to notice compulsive night scrolling and setting a limit.

passage:
In the hostel study hall, Gautam, sixteen, dozed off with his head on his chemistry book. Warden Sarita Ma'am tapped the desk. "Third time this week."
"Sorry, ma'am. Couldn't sleep."
She sat down beside him. "Couldn't, or didn't?"
Gautam thought about the night before: one reel, then another, then a gaming match that ended at 2:40. He'd told himself "five more minutes" at least six times.
"Didn't," he admitted. "I don't even enjoy it after midnight. I just can't stop."
Sarita Ma'am nodded. "What would help you stop?"
He thought. "If the phone's not near the bed. And if I stop the game at eleven, even mid-match."
That night he left his phone charging at the warden's desk. His roommate Aarav laughed at him. By Friday, Aarav's phone was charging there too.

qa.q: What time did Gautam's gaming match end the night before?
qa.a: It ended at 2:40.

qa.q: What was Gautam feeling when he admitted "I just can't stop"?
qa.a: Gautam felt frustrated and a bit ashamed, knowing the late-night scrolling no longer felt good but struggling to stop.

qa.q: What did Sarita Ma'am do well in this conversation?
qa.a: She asked questions instead of scolding, so Gautam named the problem himself and chose his own limits.

qa.q: Why might Aarav go from laughing to charging his phone there too?
qa.a: Aarav may have noticed Gautam sleeping better and realised he had the same problem, so the joke turned into a shared habit.

grounding: Shows a teenager noticing compulsive late-night phone use and setting his own limits.
